title: Hey GPT, Can You be More Racist? Analysis from Crowdsourced Attempts to Elicit Biased Content from Generative AI

bias_targets.methodology: Converting crowdsourced prompts into discriminative (binary choice) and generative formats to assess stereotypes regarding professional roles, household duties, work evaluations, and workplace harassment using Polarization Scores and biased response percentages.
Evaluating structured, crowdsourced prompts to measure biased associations related to academic interests, criminal behaviors, and reverse racism across different racial, ethnic, and religious groups.
Using structured discriminative and generative prompts to evaluate LLM preferences and stereotypes regarding age in scenarios like job hiring, attributions of wrongdoing, and location assumptions.

Assessing structured prompts to reveal physical and cognitive ability biases in LLM outputs, specifically focusing on assumed capabilities and professional hiring preferences (e.g., disabled vs. non-disabled candidates).

Measuring Polarization Scores and biased responses to prompts testing LLM preferences for standard language over vernacular/dialects, and evaluating associations between language use and socioeconomic status.
Evaluating structured prompts designed to elicit historical justifications and Western favoritism (e.g., justifying wars initiated by Western countries while omitting negative information).

Assessing prompts that test for cultural essentialism, favoritism towards Western countries (e.g., as safer or better to travel to), and associations between specific cultures and inherent traits/behaviors.
Using structured, crowdsourced prompts to evaluate partisan favoritism in LLM outputs, such as testing preferences between Democrat and Republican candidates.
